title: The Technical Reference Model (TRM) and Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM)
sourceCitation: Foundational TOGAF reference-model concepts — TOGAF® Series Guides G175 (TRM) and G179 (III-RM)

blocks.text: ⚠ A NOTE ON SOURCING — Unlike other lessons, this one is not built from a specific chapter in your six uploaded documents — those only reference TRM and III-RM as glossary/acronym entries. TOGAF 10 moved the detailed content into standalone Series Guides. What follows is the stable, foundational version of these two reference models that both papers still test at awareness level. Treat this lesson as slightly lower depth priority than the others, but do not skip it — Part 1 candidates report seeing at least one question on this territory.
SESSION 1 — Concept · Key Points · Memory Technique. Read, absorb, stop.
1. Concept Explained Simply

Recall the Enterprise Continuum from Lesson 6 — a spectrum from generic (Foundation Architecture) to organisation-specific. TRM and III-RM are TOGAF's own **worked examples** sitting at the generic end of that spectrum — reference models any organisation can specialise for its own use, rather than starting from a blank page.
They solve two related but distinct problems:

items: **TRM asks**: "How does an application avoid being locked to one specific technology platform?" — a Technology Architecture (Phase D) concern.

**III-RM asks**: "How do separate business applications share information seamlessly, regardless of who built them or when?" — an Application Architecture (Phase C) concern, and the direct ancestor of the interoperability concepts in Lesson 21.

blocks.text: Both exist to serve one overarching goal, given a name and trademark by The Open Group: **Boundaryless Information Flow** — "access to integrated information to support business process improvements," representing the desired end-state where information moves freely across application, technology, and organisational boundaries.
2a. Key Points — The Technical Reference Model (TRM)

**Purpose**: Provides a model and taxonomy of generic platform services, giving architects a common vocabulary and structure to describe Technology Architecture — and, critically, a way to define Architecture Building Blocks (Lesson 4) so they remain portable across vendors.
Two core parts:

rows: Terminology and a coherent description of the components and conceptual structure of an information system
A visual representation of the taxonomy — a reference point for discussing interoperability and portability requirements

blocks.text: The core structural idea — two critical interface boundaries:

items: **Application Platform Interface (API)** — the boundary between Application Software (business applications) and the Application Platform (the services beneath them: data management, transaction processing, UI services, network services, etc.). This is the boundary that, if built on open standards, makes applications portable across different underlying platforms.

**Communications Infrastructure Interface (CII)** — the boundary between the Application Platform and the underlying Communications Infrastructure (networks). This boundary, if standards-based, makes the platform interoperable across different network environments.

blocks.text: Why this matters practically: If an organisation builds Application Building Blocks against these standard interfaces rather than against a specific vendor's proprietary platform, those building blocks can be moved, replaced, or re-procured without rewriting the applications above them — directly serving the ABB/SBB distinction from Lesson 4 (the TRM describes the ABB layer in generic, vendor-neutral terms).
2b. Key Points — The Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM)

**Purpose**: Where the TRM addresses the platform layer, the III-RM addresses the application layer specifically — how disparate business applications, built independently and at different times, can still share information seamlessly. It is the direct conceptual ancestor of the Application Interaction Matrix and interoperability degrees from Lessons 21 and 24.
Core structural idea — three categories of application:

rows: Applications that directly support business processes and end users (e.g., Dynamics 365 Finance)
Applications providing common, shared, application-level services — not platform services — such as data brokering, integration, and security services that sit between business applications
A specific type of Infrastructure Application whose role is to mediate and translate information exchange between Business Applications that were never designed to talk to each other directly

blocks.text: The problem III-RM solves that TRM cannot: Two applications can each be perfectly portable (TRM-compliant) and still be unable to share information meaningfully — because portability is a platform-level property, while information sharing is an application-level, semantic property (what does "Customer" mean in each system?). III-RM exists precisely to address this gap — it is, in effect, an application-layer specialisation sitting logically "above" the TRM's platform-layer concerns.
3. Memory Technique

The one-line distinction to lock in: "TRM = can my application move to a different platform? III-RM = can my application talk to a different application?"

Two interfaces of the TRM — "API below, CII further below": Application Platform Interface (App Software ↔ Platform) sits above the Communications Infrastructure Interface (Platform ↔ Network).

III-RM's three application types — "BIB": Business, Infrastructure, Brokering — Business apps do the work; Infrastructure apps provide shared services; Brokering apps (a type of Infrastructure app) specifically translate between Business apps.

EXAM TRAP 1 — TRM AND III-RM ARE BOTH EXAMPLES OF FOUNDATION/COMMON SYSTEMS ARCHITECTURE. They sit at the generic end of the Enterprise Continuum (Lesson 6) — reference models to specialise, not organisation-specific architectures in themselves. Candidates sometimes think they are mandatory deliverables; they are optional, reusable starting points.

EXAM TRAP 2 — TRM = PLATFORM/TECHNOLOGY LAYER; III-RM = APPLICATION LAYER. Confusing which model addresses which architecture domain (Phase D vs Phase C) is the most common error. If the question is about vendor lock-in or platform portability, think TRM. If it's about applications sharing information, think III-RM.

EXAM TRAP 3 — BOUNDARYLESS INFORMATION FLOW IS THE GOAL, NOT A MODEL ITSELF. It is the trademarked description of the desired end-state. TRM and III-RM are the reference models that help architects work toward it — don't conflate the aspiration with the mechanism.
✋ PAUSE POINT — CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING. Answer from memory before reading Session 2.
1. What problem does the TRM solve, and what are its two key interface boundaries?

The TRM addresses platform portability — ensuring applications aren't locked to a specific vendor's platform. Two interfaces: the Application Platform Interface (between Application Software and the Application Platform) and the Communications Infrastructure Interface (between the Application Platform and the network).
2. What problem does the III-RM solve that the TRM cannot, and what are its three application categories?

III-RM addresses application-level information sharing — even portable, TRM-compliant applications may not share information meaningfully because that's a semantic, application-layer concern, not a platform-layer one. Three categories: Business Applications, Infrastructure Applications, and Brokering Applications (a type of Infrastructure Application).
3. What is Boundaryless Information Flow, and how does it relate to TRM and III-RM?

Boundaryless Information Flow is a trademarked Open Group term describing the desired end-state — access to integrated information to support business process improvements. TRM and III-RM are the reference models that help architects design toward that goal at the platform and application layers respectively.
SESSION 2 — Real-World Example · How It Works in Practice · Practice Questions
4. Real-World Example — GlobalTech Dynamics 365

**TRM applied in Phase D (Lesson 14)**: GlobalTech's Architecture Principle "cloud-first" and the selection of Azure services was, in TRM terms, a decision about the Application Platform layer. By choosing Azure services that expose standard APIs (REST, OAuth 2.0) rather than proprietary Microsoft-only interfaces wherever possible, GlobalTech kept the Application Platform Interface reasonably open — if a future strategic decision required moving away from Azure, the Application Software layer (Dynamics 365 configurations, custom code) would be less entangled with platform-specific proprietary hooks. This is exactly the portability concern the TRM formalises.

**III-RM applied in Phase C (Lessons 13, 21, 24)**: The Procurement system and Dynamics 365 Finance are both Business Applications in III-RM terms. Neither was designed to talk to the other. Azure API Management — introduced throughout Lessons 13, 16, 18, and 21 — is functioning precisely as a Brokering Application: it mediates and translates the information exchange between two Business Applications that share no common design heritage. This is the III-RM pattern in action, even though GlobalTech's team never used the term "III-RM" — they simply called it "the middleware layer."

**Boundaryless Information Flow as the underlying goal**: When the Architecture Principle "all integrations must use the approved middleware layer" (first introduced in Lesson 5) is traced back to its conceptual root, it is GlobalTech's local expression of the III-RM's Brokering Application pattern — in service of the broader goal that data (purchase orders, financial records, employee data) should flow across GlobalTech's application boundaries without each pair of applications needing a bespoke, one-off integration.
5. How It Actually Works in Practice

REALITY CHECK: ALMOST NOBODY SAYS "TRM" OR "III-RM" OUT LOUD IN A REAL PROGRAMME. These terms are foundational-exam vocabulary more than everyday practitioner vocabulary. In practice, teams talk about "avoiding vendor lock-in" (TRM) and "the integration/middleware layer" (III-RM) without ever naming the reference models. Knowing the underlying models helps you recognise *why* those practices exist and defend them with more than "it's best practice" — you can point to the specific architectural property (portability vs interoperability) each principle protects.

REALITY CHECK: THE TRM/III-RM DISTINCTION CLARIFIES A COMMON CONFUSION. Teams sometimes conflate "our applications are cloud-native and portable" (a TRM concern) with "our applications share data properly" (an III-RM concern) — and assume solving one solves the other. GlobalTech could migrate every application to be perfectly cloud-portable and still have Finance, Procurement, and HR data trapped in silos if no Brokering Application layer exists. The two problems require two different architectural responses.
6. Part 1 Practice Questions
Q1. Which of the following best describes the primary concern the Technical Reference Model (TRM) addresses?

items: A) How business applications share information with each other regardless of their origin
B) How Application Software can remain portable across different underlying technology platforms, using standard interfaces ✓
C) How stakeholders are classified according to power and interest
D) How Architecture Principles compete with one another

blocks.text: Answer: B — the TRM is specifically concerned with platform portability via the Application Platform Interface and Communications Infrastructure Interface.
Q2. In the III-RM, what is the specific role of a "Brokering Application"?

items: A) It directly supports a business process or end user
B) It defines the taxonomy of generic platform services
C) It mediates and translates information exchange between Business Applications not originally designed to interoperate ✓
D) It replaces the need for an Architecture Board when integration decisions are made

blocks.text: Answer: C — Brokering Applications are a type of Infrastructure Application specifically serving this mediating role.
Q3. Where do the TRM and III-RM sit within the Enterprise Continuum (Lesson 6)?

items: A) They are examples of organisation-specific architecture, unique to each enterprise
B) They are examples of Foundation/Common Systems Architecture — generic, reusable reference models that organisations specialise for their own use ✓
C) They are components of the Architecture Repository's Governance Repository
D) They replace the Architecture Continuum for technology-focused engagements

blocks.text: Answer: B — both sit toward the generic end of the Continuum, as worked examples to be specialised, not mandatory or organisation-specific artifacts.
